summary:
El Salvador has no Gender Identity Law and no legal mechanism by which a visitor or resident can obtain official recognition of gender identity. In 2022 the Constitutional Chamber of the Supreme Court ordered reform of the Name Law to permit name changes matching gender identity, holding the existing rules unconstitutional as gender-based discrimination, but as of 2023 the Legislative Assembly had enacted nothing, so official papers still cannot be updated. The case had originated in a 2016 lawsuit filed by a transgender activist.

The penal framework contains an enhanced penalty for bias-motivated killing. In September 2015 the National Assembly approved reforms under which homicides motivated by sexual orientation, race, ethnicity, political affiliation or gender carry 30 to 60 years under Article 129 of the penal code. The same year's hate-crime provisions added sexual orientation and gender identity grounds to the Criminal Code with penalties of three to six years' imprisonment.

The limits of that framework are illustrated by the killing of Camila Díaz Córdova, a trans Salvadoran woman deported from the United States and killed in January 2019. On 28 July 2020 a San Salvador judge found three police officers guilty of her murder and sentenced each to 20 years. It was the first homicide conviction in El Salvador for the killing of a transgender person, and Human Rights Watch described the judgment as pivotal for transgender Salvadorans' rights. Reporting at the time framed the prosecution as an advance toward the country's first hate-crime homicide conviction while documenting continuing discrimination and abuse of LGBT citizens.

Killing and abuse of LGBT people are documented over decades rather than isolated. A peer-reviewed longitudinal study published in 2024 profiles the crimes, victims and perpetrators of homicides against LGBTI+ people in El Salvador across 2000 to 2020. Human Rights Watch reported in October 2020, and again in a full report in January 2021, that El Salvador fails to address violence and entrenched discrimination against LGBT people effectively, setting out obstacles to obtaining protection and recommending action to the president, attorney general, congress and ministries. Roughly 500 hate crimes against LGBT people were reported between 1998 and 2015, with many more unreported; police have shown a blatant refusal to cooperate in LGBT death investigations, and gang violence includes targeting of LGBT people through physical and sexual assault, forced recruitment and extortion for protection.

Detention carries acute risk. Since the state of exception began in March 2022, trans women captured in mass raids have been held in the ordinary prison system with no gender-identity accommodation. One woman arrested in San Salvador on 14 April 2022 was held first at police lockups and then in prison, where custodians forcibly shaved her hair, singled her out with another trans woman for outdoor punishment drills while handcuffed and forced to squat in the sun, and denied her access to the HIV clinic; a judge released her after about four months, finding the arrest unsupported, while the other woman remains imprisoned. Socorro Jurídico Humanista and Cristosal link such abuse to the absence of a Gender Identity Law, and reporting documents placement by birth sex in the general prison system with trans-targeted abuse and no special custody provision.

Prison conditions are explicitly hostile to gender non-conformity. Homosexual inmates are forbidden from dressing or behaving in an effeminate manner, and men are targeted by police officers, soldiers and prison guards for effeminate behaviour or dress through unwarranted searches, theft of property, sexual assault and other physical violence. In a 1999 investigation concerning two transvestite detainees, the two were forced to wear men's clothing for their hearing.

Healthcare access is restricted and frequently discriminatory. Hospital specialists commonly dismiss trans patients' problems as a side effect of being transgender, and patients are sometimes made to wait longer or denied care, a pattern that can be applied discreetly. There is a lack of protocols and programmes for hormone therapy and sex reassignment surgery, and one study found that many trans women did not seek medical help after suffering post-surgical side effects, having learned not to trust the system. Psychological care is reported as insecure and prejudiced, and is often delivered as conversion therapy, frequently deployed by parents; LGBT community members report suicide ideation and attempts at higher rates than the general population.

Partner recognition does not exist. The Family Code's Article 11 defines marriage as a heterosexual union, same-sex couples cannot adopt as a couple, and the Law on Family Violence does not apply to same-sex couples. Since 2006 there have been proposals to amend the Constitution to restrict recognition even of same-sex couples married legally abroad. Two challenges to the marriage ban were dismissed on technical and procedural grounds, on 20 December 2016 and 17 January 2019, although the Constitutional Court declared a proposed marriage ban unlawful in January 2018 and admitted a lawsuit on recognition of same-sex marriage for hearing in August 2019, following the January 2018 Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion holding same-sex marriage to be a human right.

Social hostility is measurable and shapes street-level risk. A 2013 study found that 62% of Salvadorans do not accept homosexuality and 85% believe it acceptable to attack a transgender individual on the basis of their identity. Church leaders have organised opposition to LGBT rights legislation, and an embedded machismo culture treats being Salvadoran as virile and heterosexual, with 'gay friendly' regarded as against nature, anti-religious and anti-masculine.
tangentialFactors:
El Salvador's failure to address anti-LGBT violence is assessed alongside Guatemala and Honduras in Human Rights Watch's October 2020 reporting, which found that the same pattern of entrenched discrimination and inadequate protection drives asylum claims to the United States. Regional jurisprudence matters here: the January 2018 Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion on same-sex marriage prompted the Salvadoran Constitutional Court's own actions in 2018 and 2019, but produced no change in domestic law.

Public opinion constrains reform. A 2010 poll showed 10% support for legalising same-sex marriage and the 2017 AmericasBarometer recorded 19%. Over half of Salvadorans identify as actively practising Catholics and many of the remainder attend evangelical churches, both of which have been mobilised against LGBT rights legislation.

Education and family environment shape the risk landscape for younger visitors and residents. Sexuality is absent from school curriculum, leading many LGBT students to remain invisible at school to avoid discrimination; students whose gender expression does not match that assigned at birth drop out at high rates and some have been expelled outright for their sexuality and identity. Where LGBT children do come out, families may subject them to conversion therapy or family prayers, and where these fail, some families expel the child and sever contact.

No known universities or graduate programmes in the country offer Sexuality Studies; academic publications exist, most from the University of El Salvador, generally from psychological or legal science perspectives, with varying levels of internal support.
localsOnly:
Residents have a formal, if unimplemented, route to redress. The 2022 Constitutional Chamber order on the Name Law remains the operative judicial finding, and the 2018 Institutional Policy for the Care of the LGBT Population allows LGBT people to file legal complaints against discrimination.

Health-sector protections exist on paper. In April 2009 the Ministry of Public Health and Social Assistance published guidelines banning discrimination against LGBT and HIV-positive people in health services; a 2009 national HIV/AIDS health plan included a prohibition on sexual orientation-based discrimination in health care; and a national HIV/AIDS policy has been in development since 2005, with the first National HIV testing day established in 2007. Gay and bisexual men are permitted to donate blood, though policy prohibits those who engage in 'risky behaviours' from donating.

Community organising has a long record. Entre Amigos organised the country's first Gay Pride Parade in June 1997 to commemorate the massacre of trans women in the 1980s, and it continues annually; San Salvador authorised permanent rainbow paintings at several crossroads in July 2017.

Advocacy organisations active on detention abuse include Socorro Jurídico Humanista and Cristosal, which document the absence of a Gender Identity Law as the structural cause of trans women's treatment in the prison system.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory addresses entry, visa or border-screening practice for trans travellers, including whether passport gender markers inconsistent with presentation are questioned on arrival. That gap is unresolved rather than cleared.

Whether the three-to-six-year penalty added to the Criminal Code in 2015 has ever been applied is not sourced here; the only documented prosecution resulting in a conviction is the July 2020 judgment in the Camila Díaz Córdova case.

Implementation of the 2022 Constitutional Chamber order on the Name Law after 2023 is not sourced. The inventory establishes the order and the absence of legislative action as of 2023, and nothing later.

Figures on hate crimes cover 1998 to 2015 and are reported figures only; the inventory itself notes substantial underreporting, and no official count for the state-of-exception period beginning March 2022 is available here.

Current street-level enforcement practice against trans people outside detention, and any change in police cooperation with LGBT death investigations since the 2020 reporting, are not sourced.
